extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in standards for epic poetry and polite-periodical conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and standards for composing and judging epic (heroic) poetry (and incidental social-etiquette notes from a periodical). Emphasizes fable/plot structure, characterization, sentiments, and language/style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable structure: simple vs implex
rubrics_metrics.description: The fable of every poem is either simple (no change of fortune) or implex (the chief actor's fortune changes from bad to good or good to bad). The implex fable is thought most perfect because it stirs up the passions and provides a greater variety of accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implex fables come in two kinds: (1) the hero rises through dangers to honour and prosperity (e.g. Ulysses); (2) the hero falls from honour into misery (e.g. Oedipus). The latter is particularly effective for tragedy. The critic regards the presence or absence of an appropriate fable-structure as a major imperfection when mismatched to genre (e.g. Paradise Lost's unhappy event is an imperfection for a heroic poem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate conception and role of the hero
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic poem should present a central action and figure appropriate to the genre; the hero ought to suit the type of epic intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poem is called heroic but its supposed hero is unsuccessful (as some accused Milton's Adam of being), that is cause for objection; the true hero in such a poem may be another figure (Addison proposes the Messiah as the proper hero of Paradise Lost). Match the chief actor and primary action to the expectations of the epic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and plausibility of incidents (especially allegorical actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular incidents or personified allegories in an epic should have sufficient probability for the poem's scale and mode; improbable actions weaken the epic dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing implausible or overly fanciful acts to allegorical figures (Addison cites the actions ascribed to Sin and Death, and the picture of the Limbo of Vanity, as lacking probability and more akin to Spenser/Ariosto than Homer/Virgil). Allegorical passages should fit the epic's tone and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive digressions and authorial intrusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The epic poet should minimize digressions and the author's own reflections that interrupt the narrative flow; the story should generally be delivered by the characters or actors within the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's precept: authors should seldom speak themselves but throw as much as possible into the mouths of principal actors (Homer/Virgil model). Long reflections or frequent departures from the story (personal complaints, panegyrics, unnecessary learned digressions) make the narrative less effective, though beautiful digressions may be tolerated sparingly (Milton's digressions are beautiful but still exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of pointed wit and avoidance of puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments should not be too pointed or degenerate into puns; over-pointed lines diminish the seriousness of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'too much pointed' sentiments and punning in serious epic passages (Addison cites specific lines he deems like puns). Keep the register grave where the subject demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of mythic/allusive references
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusions (especially to heathen fables) must be consistent with the poem's primary subject; presenting pagan fables as truth in a divine/religious epic is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions are acceptable when the poet frames them as fabulous; presenting pagan myths as literal truth in a divine subject is inappropriate. Ensure mythic references harmonize with the theological or epic frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty in displaying learning (avoid ostentatious erudition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should avoid unnecessary ostentation of learning; the learned material should appear integrated and natural rather than displayed for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer and Virgil conceal learning indirectly within their works; Milton's excursions into free-will, history, astronomy, geography, and technical terms sometimes reveal an ambition to show off his knowledge. Learning should inform poetry subtly rather than dominate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and naturalness of language (avoid over-laboured/obscure diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's language should not be so laboured or obscured by archaic words, transpositions, and foreign idioms that ordinary readers cannot apprehend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While sublime ideas may tempt difficult phrasing, a great poet should make hard things intelligible and not rely excessively on obsolete or foreign constructions that obscure meaning. Addison acknowledges Milton's sublime ideas but warns against letting language sink under them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of jingle/repetitive word-play in elevated poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitive or jingling phrases (e.g. 'a World of Woe', 'brought into the World a World of Woe') are poor and trifling in serious epic style and generally to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though some rhetorical authorities list such figures as beauties, contemporary polite writing largely rejects this manner; use such devices sparingly and only where truly effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize use of technical terms and terms of art
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should not be overburdened with technical vocabulary from arts and sciences; poetry should render abstruse subjects in easy, comprehensible language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical words (e.g. larboard, eccentrick, trepidation, architrave) risk making poetry feel learned rather than inspired. The knowledge presented should seem born with the poet or inspired, not merely quoted from manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative economy: use of actor-voice over poet-voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Let principal characters deliver as much of the poem's content as possible, rather than relying on the poet's voice to narrate or moralize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and examples from Homer/Virgil show greater imaginative elevation when characters speak for themselves. Avoid excessive authorial commentary; where an authorial remark is essential to the action, make it brief and relevant (Virgil's purposeful reflection in Book X is an example of a justified exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontispiece motto usage: prefer legible classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: When prefacing periodical papers with classical mottos, consider the audience's ability to read and appreciate them; Latin may be preferred over Greek for legibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correspondent complains female readers dislike Greek mottos and prefer Latin, which—while still obscure—more closely resembles their mother tongue and can be read with a spelling-book. Choose classical ornamentation that the intended readership can at least visually recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window-behaviour in polite society (light social rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lady may look out of her window at the same man twice without being supposed to have intent; repeated, prolonged signalling may be read as encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to a playful question, the periodical's advice is brief: 'Twice.'—an instruction about moderation in attention to particular observers. (Social, humorous guidance rather than formal rule.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing etiquette: avoid disrupting others
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person's dancing is merely out of time but not disruptive they may continue; if they have no ear and interrupt others, they should refrain (sit still).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the pleasure of others: amusements that make one ridiculous at others' expense should be curtailed; measure whether one's capers disturb the company before persisting.
